Saint Mary’s enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 27-5 overall and 16-2 in West Coast Conference play, tied with Gonzaga atop the league standings; ESPN’s team page lists the Gaels as 27-5 and first in the WCC standings table at 16-2, and Saint Mary’s drew No. 10 Texas A&M in the Round of 64 on March 19, 2026. Their profile is still the same Bennett-era profile in broad strokes—half-court, execution, rebounding, defense—but this year’s team has been more offensively explosive than many past Gaels teams, averaging 78.2 points per game while allowing 64.6, with 40.3 rebounds per game. Saint Mary’s was also the No. 2 seed in the 2026 WCC tournament and lost its semifinal to Santa Clara, 76-71, on March 9, 2026. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2608/saint-mary%27s-gaels))

Offensively, the first thing that shows up on film and in the numbers is how much Saint Mary’s plays through its frontcourt touch game and second-shot pressure. In Saint Mary’s own February game notes, Andrew McKeever ranked first in the WCC with 259 rebounds and 3.64 offensive rebounds per game, while Paulius Murauskas led the WCC in total points with 534 and free throws made with 151 as of February 18. That tells you what the tape confirms: they want to throw it inside, drive it into contact, and punish you on the glass. Against Oregon State on January 21, the Gaels scored 36 paint points and 16 second-chance points in an 81-51 win; against Santa Clara in the January 17 loss, they still generated 36 paint points even while losing 62-54. In other words, their offense is not built primarily on random jump shooting; it is built on interior catches, duck-ins, offensive rebounds, and guards feeding the post or probing to create kick-out threes. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/documents/download/2026/2/19/MBB_Game_Notes_25-26_at_Washington_State.pdf))

Specific actions: Saint Mary’s repeatedly uses high ball screens for Joshua Dent, horns-style entries to get a big touching the ball at the elbow, and inside-out sequences for Mikey Lewis on the weak side. You can see the result pattern in games. On February 11 against Pepperdine, Saint Mary’s posted 24 assists in an 88-60 win, with Dent tying his career high with 11 assists; that is a classic Bennett marker, because when the ball reverses side-to-side and the bigs screen into re-screen action, Dent becomes the organizer and the possession ends with a layup, a paint touch, or a rhythm three. On January 10 against Washington State, the Gaels hit a season-high 14 threes in an 88-82 win, and a 12-2 run generated solely by Mikey Lewis over 3:10 put the game away. On February 28 against Gonzaga, the Spokesman-Review’s recap explicitly described an “avalanche of 3-pointers” in Saint Mary’s 70-59 win, which is the clearest example of their adjustment from old-school grinder to selective spacing team: they still want control, but they now have perimeter shotmaking once the defense collapses. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/news/2026/2/11/mens-basketball-mbb-gaels-notch-program-record-24th-consecutive-home-victory-down-pepperdine-88-60))

Defensively, this is still a Randy Bennett team first and foremost. Saint Mary’s game notes listed the Gaels at 40.2% opponent field-goal percentage, second in the WCC and 21st nationally as of February 18. The philosophy is clear on film: shrink gaps, keep the ball in front, finish possessions with rebounds, and make opponents score late in the clock over size. Their February 28 win over Gonzaga is the cleanest evidence; Saint Mary’s held Gonzaga to 59 points, and the Saint Mary’s recap noted the Gaels became the first team to hold Gonzaga under 60 points all season. Against Oregon State, they allowed only 51. Against North Texas earlier in the season, they won 80-49. This is not an over-gambling defense; it is a disciplined shell built to choke off first actions, force contested twos, and then clean the glass. McKeever’s rebounding volume matters here just as much as Murauskas’ scoring. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/documents/download/2026/2/19/MBB_Game_Notes_25-26_at_Washington_State.pdf))

Bennett’s coaching philosophy remains possession control and game-to-game adaptation rather than stylistic stubbornness. The documented in-game adjustment history this season is strong. On January 4 against Seattle U, Saint Mary’s trailed by five at halftime, then used an 8-0 run to take control and closed the final 4:30 on an 18-5 run to win 93-76. On February 21 at Washington State, the Cougars pushed the Gaels in the first half, but Saint Mary’s answered with an 11-3 push late in the half and controlled the second half in an 83-67 road win. On January 10 against Washington State, when the Cougars cut it to one possession, Bennett’s group answered with the Lewis-led 12-2 burst. The negative example also matters: in the March 9 WCC semifinal loss to Santa Clara, a game with six ties and 14 lead changes, Saint Mary’s could not find the final counter late and lost 76-71. That game is useful for scouts because it showed that when opponents can match their physicality and make tough perimeter shots late, the Gaels are more vulnerable than in a typical grinder. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/news/2026/1/4/mens-basketball-mbb-huge-second-half-charges-gaels-to-93-76-victory-over-seattle-u))

Clutch and late-game execution has generally been good, though not flawless. The best positive example is February 18 at Seattle U, where ESPN lists a 72-70 Saint Mary’s win; that is exactly the type of two-possession game the Gaels usually survive because Dent can manage tempo and they are elite at the foul line. Another is January 10 versus Washington State, when Lewis’ solo 12-2 takeover turned a one-possession game into a finishable cushion in an 88-82 win. February 14 at Pacific is another useful tape: Saint Mary’s won 72-61 after a second-half surge, with Murauskas posting a 32-point, 15-rebound masterpiece according to the February 19 game notes. The warning signs are Boise State’s 68-67 win on December 14 and Santa Clara’s 76-71 semifinal win on March 9; both games showed that if Saint Mary’s is dragged into a possession-for-possession late clock shotmaking contest without separation on the glass, they can be beaten. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2608/saint-mary%27s-gaels))

Key players start with Paulius Murauskas, the offensive fulcrum. ESPN lists him at 18.8 points per game, and Saint Mary’s game notes had him at 534 points through February 18, first in the WCC. His standout recent moment was the 32-point, 15-rebound game at Pacific on February 14. He also scored 26 points with eight rebounds in the March 9 loss to Santa Clara and had 30 points and 15 rebounds in the January 4 win over Seattle U. He is the matchup problem because he can score on the block, draw fouls, and step out enough to keep slower bigs honest. Joshua Dent is the organizer: ESPN lists him at 5.7 assists per game, while Saint Mary’s listed him at 174 assists, 5.6 per game, and a WCC-leading 91.8% free-throw rate area figure of 91.8%/91.8 FT percentage? More precisely, Saint Mary’s listed Dent at 91.8% from the line and 36:07 per game in the March 3 all-conference release. His biggest scoring spike came with a career-high 26 points against Washington State on January 10, and he tied his career high with 11 assists against Pepperdine on February 11. Mikey Lewis is the microwave scorer turned full-time starting weapon. Saint Mary’s March 2 release named him the final WCC Player of the Week, and the all-conference release described him as having “found his stride as an elite scoring guard.” He scored 22 at Washington State on February 21, 20 against Washington State on January 10, and authored the decisive 12-2 personal run in that January win. Andrew McKeever is the glass-and-rim piece; Saint Mary’s had him first in the WCC in rebounds and offensive rebounds per game as of February 18, and he posted 14 points and 14 rebounds against San Francisco on February 7. Harry Wessels is the veteran interior body whose value is more structural than statistical—screening, length, defensive positioning, and finishing. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2608/saint-mary%27s-gaels))

The notable wins tell you the ceiling. Beating No. 9 Gonzaga 70-59 on February 28 revealed the elite version of Saint Mary’s: disciplined half-court defense, enough shooting to punish tags, and the ability to keep a high-end offense under 60. Winning 83-67 at Washington State on February 21 showed road composure and offensive versatility, especially with Dent scoring 22 and the team hitting 10 threes. The 88-60 win over Pepperdine on February 11 showed how deadly they are when the ball is moving; 24 assists is not accidental. The notable losses show the pressure points. Vanderbilt’s 96-71 win in the Battle 4 Atlantis title game on November 28 revealed that Saint Mary’s can get overwhelmed by high-end athletic pace and scoring bursts. Boise State’s 68-67 win on December 14 exposed their vulnerability in coin-flip late games outside the WCC. Santa Clara’s 76-71 WCC semifinal win on March 9 showed a team that could match Saint Mary’s physicality and survive the half-court knife fight with late shotmaking. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/news/2026/3/1/mens-basketball-mbb-senior-night-victory-rivalry-victory-championship-victory-gaels-defeat-no-9-gonzaga-70-59-to-clinch-fourth-straight-wcc-title?utm_source=openai))

As for Bennett’s NCAA tournament history, Saint Mary’s official coaching bio is clear. He first took Saint Mary’s to the NCAA tournament in 2005, returned in 2008, reached the Sweet 16 in 2010 with wins over Richmond and Villanova, and Saint Mary’s reached the second round for the fifth time in his tenure by winning in the 2025 NCAA tournament. The bio also notes 2012 and 2017 as program-best No. 7 seeds, while the 2022-23 team made the second round, giving Bennett multiple eras of tournament success. So the shorthand is: one Sweet 16 under Bennett in 2010, multiple second-round appearances, and a long track record of getting Saint Mary’s to March with a team that travels because it defends, rebounds, and executes. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/randy-bennett/2569))

Saint Mary’s enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as one of the more statistically interesting teams in the field: strong enough across predictive systems to profile like a protected-seed caliber team in pure quality, but with a résumé and schedule context that mute the public perception. The broadest picture is this: Saint Mary’s finished the regular-season / conference-tournament window at roughly 26-5 to 27-5 depending on source update timing, won the WCC regular season, and sat well inside the national top tier of predictive rankings even though its schedule strength was merely moderate by at-large contender standards. ESPN’s BPI had Saint Mary’s 5th nationally as of March 18, 2026, an extremely aggressive rating that implies the Gaels were viewed as one of the best teams in the country on a possession-by-possession basis going into the bracket. WarrenNolan’s team page listed Saint Mary’s with a live RPI of 14, while its NET strength-of-schedule page placed the Gaels 94th nationally in overall NET SOS and 126th in non-conference SOS. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi?utm_source=openai))

That split is the core of the Saint Mary’s profile: the predictive systems liked them more than résumé-based framing or narrative shorthand would suggest. Sports-Reference’s 2025-26 team page lists Saint Mary’s at 78.2 points scored per game and just 64.6 allowed, with a Simple Rating System of 18.12 and strength of schedule of 5.80, which ranked 88th nationally. On the efficiency side, Sports-Reference posted a team offensive rating of 117.6 points per 100 possessions and a defensive rating of 97.1, yielding about a +20.5 net efficiency margin. WarrenNolan’s advanced net rating page similarly showed Saint Mary’s at +19.8, which corroborates the same basic conclusion: this was a comfortably top-25-level efficiency team and, depending on the model, closer to top-10 quality than top-25 quality. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/saint-marys-ca/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

If you map that against the requested ranking buckets, the cleanest verified numbers I could find are: BPI No. 5 nationally, live RPI No. 14, NET SOS No. 94, non-conference NET SOS No. 126, and opponent/game pages that identify Gonzaga as NET No. 7 and Santa Clara as NET No. 40 within Saint Mary’s schedule context. I was able to verify that Saint Mary’s itself was in the high-end national cluster on team sheets and bracket placement, but a directly accessible official NCAA team-sheet page with the exact Saint Mary’s NET integer was not exposed cleanly in the search results. Based on the bracket context, WarrenNolan team page, and quality-opponent listings, the Gaels clearly sat in the tournament-safe range and likely in the approximate top-20 to top-30 NET band, but I will stick to the exact values I could directly verify rather than invent an integer. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Saint-Marys-College&utm_source=openai))

The shooting and possession profile helps explain why the computers were so high on them. Sports-Reference season totals show Saint Mary’s shooting 46.1% from the floor, 38.9% from three, and 80.5% from the foul line across 32 games, with 260 made threes on 669 attempts. That gives them an exact three-point attempt rate of 669/1847 = 36.2% of field-goal attempts, and an exact effective field-goal percentage of (852 + 0.5*260) / 1847 = 53.1%. Those are strong offensive indicators: not ultra-bombing from deep, but definitely perimeter-capable, and highly efficient once free throws are included. NCAA stat snapshots from February also had Saint Mary’s 11th nationally in three-point percentage at 38.79% and 23rd in three-point attempts per game at 29.7, reinforcing the identity of a disciplined half-court offense that still generates enough volume from outside to punish help. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

The free-throw profile is especially notable. From the Sports-Reference totals, Saint Mary’s attempted 668 free throws against 1847 field-goal attempts, an exact FT rate of 0.362. That is a healthy figure for a team often stereotyped as simply slow and grindy. In other words, this offense was not just working late-clock motion into contested jumpers; it also produced pressure and conversion at the line. Combined with 80.5% team free-throw shooting, that makes Saint Mary’s a high-floor late-game team and one less vulnerable to variance than a pure jump-shooting squad. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

Turnovers look more mixed. Sports-Reference credits Saint Mary’s with 346 turnovers over 1847 field-goal attempts plus 668 free-throw attempts, which is not enough by itself to derive a perfectly standard KenPom-style TO% without possessions, but game logs and box-score trends suggest a generally solid rather than elite ball-security team. In several representative wins, the Gaels were very clean: only five turnovers in a 79-54 home win over San Francisco and seven in an 81-51 win over Oregon State. But the losses show where the offense can flatten out: 13 turnovers in a 54-62 loss at Santa Clara and 11 in a 65-73 loss at Gonzaga, both games where the shooting also cratered. That suggests the offensive downside is less about constant sloppiness than about what happens when a good defense can force Saint Mary’s into lower-quality threes and tougher late-clock possessions. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Saint-Marys-College))

Rebounding appears solid and probably underrated. Sports-Reference totals show 398 offensive rebounds and 1291 total rebounds in 32 games, which is 12.4 offensive boards and 40.3 total rebounds per game. NCAA stat snapshots also had Saint Mary’s at 40.11 rebounds per game in mid-February. Without a directly accessible adjusted OR% source, the best synthesis is that Saint Mary’s projects as at least good on the offensive glass and very good overall on the backboards, which fits the program’s usual physical profile. They are not just a finesse execution team; they are structurally sound in ending possessions and generating second chances. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

Pace is the hardest exact metric to verify directly from public 2026 sources, but the available evidence still points clearly in one direction: Saint Mary’s remained a slow-tempo team by national standards. Their raw offensive and defensive ratings, combined with 78.2 points scored and 64.6 allowed, imply a possession environment in the mid-60s per game rather than the high-60s or 70s. That is also consistent with the visual record of their schedule: many games played in the 60s and low 70s, with scores controlled by shot quality, rebounding, and free-throw margin rather than transition volume. So while I could not verify an exact possessions-per-40 figure from a directly accessible public leaderboard, the available evidence supports the standard Saint Mary’s conclusion: below-average pace, but not anemic offense. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/saint-marys-ca/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent form was strong overall, though not flawless. WarrenNolan’s team page listed Saint Mary’s at 8-2 over its last 10 entering the tournament window, with a one-game losing streak at the moment of that snapshot. Within that stretch, they posted several authoritative wins: 79-54 and 78-59 over San Francisco, 87-60 over San Diego, 81-51 over Oregon State, and 93-76 over Seattle. The two most telling setbacks in the broader late-season sample were the 54-62 loss at Santa Clara and the 65-73 loss at Gonzaga. Those results sharpen the scouting report: if Saint Mary’s can impose its physical half-court defense and keep the game on its terms, it looks overwhelming; if an opponent with credible size and shotmaking can drag the Gaels into lower-efficiency perimeter offense, the margin for error narrows quickly. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Saint-Marys-College&utm_source=openai))

The biggest divergence from conventional wisdom is offensive quality. The eye test for Saint Mary’s often defaults to “slow, rugged, defense-first, ugly but effective.” The data says that undersells them. A team shooting 38.9% from three, 80.5% from the line, posting a 53.1% eFG, and rating at 117.6 offensive points per 100 possessions is not merely surviving in the half court; it is executing at a high level. The stronger contrarian take is actually this: Saint Mary’s defense is excellent, but the offense is what makes the team dangerous in March because it combines spacing, free-throw reliability, and enough rebounding to avoid total dependence on hot shooting. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

The second divergence is schedule interpretation. Because the Gaels played in the WCC and had only a middling NET SOS profile, the résumé can look less imposing than that of a power-conference peer. But BPI at No. 5 and efficiency margins around +20 are the kind of signals that historically map to teams capable of beating almost anyone if the matchup is right. That does not mean Saint Mary’s was invulnerable; it means they were miscast if framed as a cute mid-major-type seed with limited upside. Statistically, the profile is closer to a bona fide second-weekend threat: elite predictive respect, top-tier defense, excellent foul shooting, very good three-point shooting, strong rebounding structure, and a pace that compresses variance and amplifies execution. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Saint Mary’s is still a classic Randy Bennett team in 2025-26: slow, half-court oriented, highly physical on the glass, and comfortable winning possession-by-possession. Their adjusted tempo was 61.7 possessions per 40 minutes, 359th of 364 nationally, and their average possession length was 20.2 seconds, fifth-longest in Division I; EvanMiya also had them 358th nationally in true tempo. They do not want a track meet. They want long offensive possessions, second-shot chances, and a game played in the 60s. Their fast-break scoring was only 6.45 points per game, 327th nationally, while their offense protected the ball at a 15.1% turnover rate and their offensive rebound rate was 40.5%, second in the country. The tactical implication is clear: the best way to disrupt Saint Mary’s is not simply “pressure them,” but to pressure them in ways that deny entry timing, make their first action start later in the clock, and then finish possessions with a clean rebound so their elite second-chance game never activates. Vanderbilt’s scout framed this well before the NCAA matchup: Saint Mary’s couples ultra-slow pace with top-end ball security and offensive rebounding, so opponents have to attack the possession chain, not just the initial action. ([vanderbilthustler.com](https://vanderbilthustler.com/2025/03/20/mens-basketball-three-stats-to-watch-vs-saint-marys/))

In personnel terms, the Gaels are unusually big across the front line. Joshua Dent is a 6-3 lead guard, Mikey Lewis a 6-3 scoring guard, Dillan Shaw a 6-7 wing/forward, Paulius Murauskas a 6-8, 235-pound power forward, and Andrew McKeever a 7-3, 285-pound center; Harry Wessels gives them another 7-1, 280-pound center body. That size creates obvious mismatches at the 4 and 5 against smaller tournament teams. Murauskas is the bruising matchup problem because he combines bulk with scoring and rebounding production, while McKeever/Wessels supply true center size. The flip side is at the point of attack: neither Dent nor Lewis is an overwhelming downhill athlete by high-major standards, and Shaw, though long at 6-7, is more connector than explosive creator. If you have an elite quick-twitch lead guard or a springy small-ball 4 who can drag Murauskas into repeated perimeter closeouts, that is where Saint Mary’s is more vulnerable than their raw rebounding numbers suggest. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/2025-26))

Their offense is much more team-based than isolation-based. Sports-Reference lists Saint Mary’s at 15.5 assists per game on 26.6 made field goals, meaning 58.3% of their made baskets are assisted. That is strong evidence of a structured, connected offense rather than an iso-heavy attack. The named exception is Mikey Lewis, who can tilt games with difficult shotmaking. In the February 28, 2026 win over Gonzaga, Lewis scored 31 points and hit 7 threes; in the March 9 WCC semifinal loss to Santa Clara, Lewis scored 23 and Murauskas 26, meaning those two supplied 49 of Saint Mary’s 71 points, or 69.0% of the offense. That game is the clearest warning sign: when you can flatten their actions and turn the game into “Lewis/Murauskas bail us out,” the offense becomes far more top-heavy than their season-long assisted-basket profile suggests. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/saint-marys-ca/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Against pressure and zone, the available evidence points to “functional but not invulnerable,” especially when pressure is paired with size at the rim or when a zone forces them to win with pure perimeter creation instead of paint touches plus offensive rebounds. The best direct evidence is the Santa Clara loss on March 9: Saint Mary’s still got 26 from Murauskas and 23 from Lewis and still won the glass by 10, yet lost 76-71. That is important because it shows you can survive their rebounding edge if you win the shot-value battle and make them play from slightly behind late. The public discussion around Saint Mary’s has also consistently identified zone/press discomfort as the style most likely to bother them, and the mechanism makes sense statistically: a slow team with long possessions is more sensitive to disruption before it gets into its first clean action. Because they do not generate much transition offense themselves, they are less able to erase ugly half-court stretches with easy run-out points. ([stmarys-ca.edu](https://www.stmarys-ca.edu/news/gaels-fall-tightly-contested-west-coast-conference-semifinal-bout-santa-clara-76-71))

Preferred pace is absolutely slow, and the way to force the opposite is specific: score before their defense gets set, make or miss; use quick outlets after defensive rebounds; and after made baskets, inbound fast and attack before Saint Mary’s can load to the ball. Gonzaga’s January 31 win, 73-65, is a useful model because Saint Mary’s was competitive but ultimately had to chase. By contrast, in the February 28 rematch Saint Mary’s flipped the script with a 15-2 second-half run and then a 12-2 run, holding Gonzaga to 23 second-half points. That game shows Bennett’s team is most dangerous when it can impose game rhythm in phases, not necessarily for 40 straight minutes but in repeated slow-down stretches that strangle momentum. Therefore, if you are trying to beat them, you must avoid dead stretches after media timeouts and start halves with pace; that is when Saint Mary’s has repeatedly made control runs. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/news/2026/1/31/mens-basketball-mbb-gaels-grind-it-out-come-up-just-short-at-no-6-gonzaga-73-65))

On transition frequency, the public stat we have is that Saint Mary’s scored only 6.45 fast-break points per game, 327th nationally, confirming transition offense is a very small slice of what they do. Defensively, the same Saint Mary’s game report against San Francisco noted that their own offensive execution “prevented the Dons from running in transition,” limiting USF to just four fast-break points and two points off turnovers. That fits the broader profile: because Saint Mary’s rarely turns it over and often sends enough size to the offensive glass while still maintaining floor balance, they are better at transition defense than their snail pace alone would imply. To create transition chances, opponents need live-ball events, long rebounds, or quick-hit early offense off makes—not just hoping for random pace. ([vanderbilthustler.com](https://vanderbilthustler.com/2025/03/20/mens-basketball-three-stats-to-watch-vs-saint-marys/))

As for coaching adaptability, Randy Bennett’s staff clearly does adjust in-game. The February 28 Gonzaga win is the cleanest example: Saint Mary’s was down at halftime, then opened the second half on a 15-2 run over the first 5:35, later added a 12-2 run, and held Gonzaga to 23 second-half points. That is a textbook adjustment game. Even in the March 9 Santa Clara loss, Saint Mary’s answered a seven-point deficit with a 12-4 run to retake the lead late, which indicates the staff can find counters during a game even when the final result goes against them. So no, this is not a rigid staff that only wins one way; Bennett’s teams are system-heavy, but they do make second-half counters. ([smcgaels.com](https://smcgaels.com/news/2026/3/1/mens-basketball-mbb-senior-night-victory-rivalry-victory-championship-victory-gaels-defeat-no-9-gonzaga-70-59-to-clinch-fourth-straight-wcc-title))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must do five things. First, gang-rebound with your guards and concede fewer than two-shot possessions; Saint Mary’s offensive rebound rate is too strong to handle with centers alone. Second, speed them up selectively—not by reckless pressing every possession, but by making them initiate offense later in the clock and then attacking immediately the other way. Third, put Murauskas and the centers in repeated screening/closeout actions so their size advantage becomes a mobility test. Fourth, top-lock or body Mikey Lewis off relocation threes and force Dent/Shaw to finish as interior scorers over length instead of allowing rhythm catch-and-shoot sequences; Lewis’s 31-point, 7-three Gonzaga game is proof that if he gets loose, the whole machine changes. Fifth, offensively, hunt early-clock scores before the Gaels build their shell. If you let the game settle into 20-second possessions, elite ball security, and 40.5% offensive rebounding, you are playing Saint Mary’s game. If you make them defend in space, rebound one-and-done, and score without second chances, they become much more beatable—as Santa Clara’s 76-71 semifinal win demonstrated even while losing the rebound margin by 10. ([vanderbilthustler.com](https://vanderbilthustler.com/2025/03/20/mens-basketball-three-stats-to-watch-vs-saint-marys/))
